t: AI, machine learning and deep learning
b: AI is the broad goal: software doing things that normally need human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is the main way to get there: instead of writing rules by hand, you show a model lots of examples and it learns the pattern. Deep learning is ML using neural networks with many layers; it powers images, speech and language. Generative AI is deep learning that creates new content (text, images, audio) rather than just labelling things. Learn the three ways a model learns. Supervised learning uses labelled examples (this email is spam, this one is not). Unsupervised learning finds groups in unlabelled data (clustering customers). Reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward (a game agent). Large language models are pre-trained on huge amounts of unlabelled text with self-supervised learning, then tuned.
an: RPGACE's taxonomy placement started as hand-written keyword rules (no learning at all). Oracle is generative AI: it writes recipes and captions rather than just picking a label. Your 5-colour ingredient status is a classification job (each ingredient gets one of a fixed set of labels), the classic supervised-learning shape.

b: Classification predicts a category (fraud or not, which genre). Regression predicts a number (house price, tomorrow's sales). Clustering groups similar things without labels (customer segments). Pick the type from the answer you want: a label means classification, a number means regression, groups with no labels mean clustering. Other common tasks are anomaly detection (spotting unusual events), recommendation (what you might like next), forecasting (numbers over time), computer vision (images) and natural language processing (text).
an: Recall's spacing (1, 3, 7, 16, 35 days) is a fixed rule, not a model. If RPGACE predicted how many days until you forget each idea, that would be regression. Sorting your Life Library onto phylum shelves is classification. Grouping beats that 'feel alike' with no labels would be clustering.

b: An ML project runs: define the business problem, collect data, prepare it (clean, label, engineer features), train, evaluate, deploy, then monitor and retrain. Data is split into training (to learn), validation (to tune) and test (to judge on data the model never saw). Garbage in, garbage out: missing, biased or unlabelled data limits any model. Features are the inputs the model uses. Hyperparameters (learning rate, number of epochs, batch size) are settings you choose before training; parameters (weights) are what the model learns. After deployment, data drift means real-world data changes so accuracy drops, which is why you monitor and retrain. MLOps is the practice of automating and repeating this lifecycle.
an: Your reference tracks are the perfect garbage-in example: the matching scorer exists, but scale and genre are filled in on 0 of 32 tracks, so 'beat matches are always the same'. No model fixes missing data. Importing 7,743 foods from 6 countries and removing duplicates was the data-preparation step.

b: For classification: accuracy is the share of all answers that were right (misleading when one class is rare). Precision: of everything the model flagged, how much was really positive (few false alarms). Recall: of all real positives, how many it caught (few misses). F1 balances precision and recall. A confusion matrix shows true/false positives and negatives. AUC-ROC measures how well it separates classes across thresholds. For regression: MAE and RMSE measure average error size; R-squared shows how much variation is explained. Overfitting = great on training data, poor on new data (memorised). Underfitting = poor on both (too simple). Business metrics (cost per user, revenue, customer satisfaction) decide if the model is worth it.
an: Pick precision when false alarms cost you: a recipe suggesting a 'substitute' that isn't one ruins dinner. Pick recall when misses cost you: a stock check that misses something you've run out of. The taxonomy engine's 1-10 confidence score with a human check below the line is the same idea as choosing a threshold.

b: Inference means using a trained model to make predictions. Real-time inference answers one request immediately with low latency (a chatbot). Batch inference (SageMaker batch transform, Bedrock batch) processes a big set of data offline when nobody is waiting, usually cheaper. Asynchronous inference queues requests with large payloads or long processing time and returns the result later. Serverless inference scales to zero when idle and suits traffic that comes and goes. Pick by latency need, payload size, traffic pattern and cost.
an: Oracle chat is real-time with streaming, so words appear as they are written. Bookworm shows the first insight straight away, then analyses the rest of the chapter in the background: that's the asynchronous pattern. The Fallback Scout queue, answered later by a scheduled routine, is batch-style. RPGACE's Vercel functions are serverless: nothing runs between requests.

t: AWS ML services you must recognise
b: Amazon SageMaker AI: build, train and deploy your own ML models (Studio, Canvas for no-code, Autopilot for AutoML, Data Wrangler for data prep, Ground Truth for labelling, Feature Store, Model Monitor for drift, Clarify for bias and explainability, JumpStart for ready-made models, Model Cards, Model Registry, Pipelines for MLOps). Pre-built AI services need no ML skills: Comprehend (text: sentiment, entities, key phrases, PII), Rekognition (images and video), Textract (text, forms and tables from documents), Transcribe (speech to text), Polly (text to speech), Translate, Lex (chatbots), Kendra (smart enterprise search), Personalize (recommendations), Augmented AI (A2I, human review of model output).
an: Your food-photo logging is Rekognition-style vision plus Textract-style label reading. Your share-a-screenshot inbox, where Oracle reads the text, is Textract's job on AWS. The jargon Review queue, where you Accept or Reject before anything counts, is exactly what Amazon A2I does for model predictions.

b: Foundation models (FMs) are huge models pre-trained on broad data and adaptable to many tasks; large language models (LLMs) are FMs for text. Text is split into tokens (pieces of words); models read and write tokens, and you pay per token. Embeddings turn text into lists of numbers (vectors) so that similar meanings sit close together. The context window is how many tokens the model can consider at once. Transformers (with attention) are the architecture behind LLMs; diffusion models generate images by removing noise step by step. Multimodal models handle more than one type: text plus images or audio. The output is probabilistic, so the same prompt can give different answers.
an: Oracle reads and writes tokens, which is why your £10 test session happened: long prompts and long answers both cost. RPGACE's session memory search uses keyword full-text search, not embeddings; with embeddings it could find 'that time we fixed the freeze' even when you type different words.

b: Generative AI is good at drafting, summarising, translating, coding help, conversation and creative work. It adapts fast and is easy to use. Its limits: hallucinations (confident but false answers), non-determinism (different answers each time), knowledge cut-off, bias from training data, lack of explainability, and cost and latency at scale. Reduce hallucinations with grounding (RAG on trusted data), clear prompts, lower temperature and human review. Inference settings: temperature (higher = more random and creative, lower = more focused), top-p and top-k (how many likely next tokens are considered), maximum tokens (length cap) and stop sequences.
an: RPGACE hit a real hallucination problem: when SELF_KNOWLEDGE went 28 days stale, Oracle confidently told you the Quest Board saved progress when it didn't. The fix was grounding: keep the facts it reads current, and check them automatically.

t: The foundation model lifecycle and costs
b: Lifecycle: data selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment and feedback. Most companies never pre-train; they pick an existing model. Choose a model on modality, task fit, quality, latency, context window, language support, licence and cost. Pricing on Amazon Bedrock is per input and output token on demand, or Provisioned Throughput (reserved capacity, needed to run a custom fine-tuned model), or batch at a lower price. Bigger is not always better: a smaller, cheaper, faster model often does a narrow job well.
an: RPGACE already runs this choice: Sonnet does judgment work, Haiku does cheap mechanical clean-up, and a different model handles outlining. That's 'right-size the model to the task'. The token-cost audit after £10 went in one test is the cost-of-generative-AI lesson in real life.

b: An AI agent is a model that plans steps, calls tools (APIs, databases, search), keeps memory and acts towards a goal, not just answers once. Multi-agent systems split work between specialised agents that pass results to each other; an orchestrator coordinates them. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting models to tools and data sources in one consistent way. On AWS: Amazon Bedrock Agents, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (runtime, memory, identity, gateway and observability for running agents securely at scale), Strands Agents (open-source agent SDK), Kiro (an agentic coding IDE), Amazon Q (business and developer assistants). Agents need guardrails, permissions and human checks because they take actions.
an: You run this every day. Claude Code reaches Supabase and Vercel through MCP connectors. Separate Claude sessions pass work through Supabase queues (openmontage_jobs), which is the multi-agent pattern. Oracle Control's confirm-before-execute popup is the human check on an agent action.

t: Choosing and customising a foundation model
b: Cheapest to most expensive way to adapt an FM: prompt engineering, then retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), then fine-tuning, then continued pre-training, then training from scratch. Prompt engineering changes only the input. RAG adds your own up-to-date documents at question time. Fine-tuning trains the model further on labelled prompt-and-answer examples to change its style or skill on a task. Continued pre-training uses large amounts of unlabelled domain text to teach it a field's language. Distillation trains a smaller 'student' model from a larger 'teacher' to cut cost and latency. Choose by cost, latency, accuracy needed, how often the data changes, and how much labelled data you have.
an: RPGACE never fine-tuned anything: it steers Oracle with prompts plus SELF_KNOWLEDGE and live facts. That's the right call for data that changes daily; fine-tuning would freeze yesterday's facts into the model.

b: RAG fetches relevant pieces of your own data at question time and adds them to the prompt, so answers are current and grounded without retraining. Steps: split documents into chunks, create embeddings, store them in a vector database, then at question time embed the question, find the closest chunks and pass them to the model. On AWS, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases manages this end to end. Vector stores include Amazon OpenSearch Service (and Serverless), Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector, Amazon Neptune Analytics and Amazon DocumentDB. Amazon Kendra can act as the retriever. RAG reduces hallucinations and lets you cite sources.
an: Ask My Data is RAG done the RPGACE way: Oracle asks for rows from 18 read-only sources (your recipes, stock, plans) with a DATA_QUERY line, gets them back and answers from them. Web lookups check your Library first, then the web. Both ground the answer in real data instead of memory.

b: A good prompt has instructions, context, input data and the output format you want. Techniques: zero-shot (no examples), few-shot (a few worked examples), chain-of-thought (ask it to reason step by step), role prompting, templates and negative instructions (what not to do). Context engineering means choosing carefully what goes into the limited context window. Risks: prompt injection (hidden instructions in content that hijack the model), jailbreaking (tricking it past its rules), prompt leaking (revealing the system prompt) and data poisoning. Defend with guardrails, input and output checks and least-privilege tools.
an: RPGACE learned the format rule the hard way: a numbered list can't survive the chat display, so features that need a list ask Oracle for one line split with ' | '. Asking for a RECIPE_JSON trailer is 'specify the output format'. The rule that content Oracle reads from the web is data, never instructions, is prompt-injection defence.

b: Judge FMs with: automatic metrics such as ROUGE (summaries, overlap with a reference), BLEU (translation), BERTScore (meaning similarity) and perplexity; benchmark datasets; human evaluation; and LLM-as-a-judge (one model grades another's answers). Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation runs automatic and human evaluations. Also check business outcomes: did it save time, raise conversion, cut cost? Test for hallucinations and grounding, and keep evaluating after launch.
an: Your smoke_test page is human evaluation: features only count as working once you tick them by hand. RPGACE's Mock Oracle mode is like evaluating the pipeline without paying for the model, and the /drift checks compare output against a pinned plan.

b: AWS's responsible AI dimensions: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance and transparency. Bias can come from unrepresentative training data, labels or how the model is used. Fix with diverse, balanced data, bias measurement, human review and monitoring. Tools: SageMaker Clarify (detects bias, explains predictions), SageMaker Model Monitor (watches quality and drift in production), Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) (human review of low-confidence predictions), Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (filters harmful content, blocks topics, redacts personal data, checks grounding), SageMaker Model Cards (documents a model's intended use and limits) and AWS AI Service Cards (AWS's own documentation of its AI services).
an: RPGACE's standing rule 'AI proposes, human confirms' is controllability and human-in-the-loop: every taxonomy write and recipe change waits for your Accept. The honest 'untested by Alex' flags everywhere are transparency.

b: Transparent or interpretable models (like a decision tree or linear regression) are easy to explain but may be less accurate. Complex models (deep neural networks, LLMs) are more powerful but harder to explain. Trade-offs: interpretability vs performance, privacy vs data detail, safety vs creativity. Explainability tools (Clarify feature attributions) show which inputs drove a prediction. Document data sources and licences (data lineage), use human-centred design, and tell users when they are dealing with AI. Legal risks of generative AI include intellectual property and copyright, biased output, loss of customer trust and hallucinated claims.
an: Your copyright rule (never pull book content from shadow-library listings) is the IP side of responsible AI. Cooking's code-computed diff, showing exactly what changed in a recipe rather than trusting the model's summary, is explainability in practice.

b: Shared responsibility model: AWS secures the cloud (hardware, data centres, managed services); you secure what you put in it (your data, access, configuration, prompts). Use AWS IAM with least privilege (roles and policies that allow only what's needed). Encrypt data at rest and in transit with AWS KMS. Keep traffic private with VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink. Store keys in AWS Secrets Manager. Amazon Macie finds sensitive data such as personal data in S3. Amazon Bedrock does not use your prompts or data to train the base models, and your data stays in the Region you choose. For agents, AgentCore Identity handles who an agent acts as and what it may access.
an: RPGACE is a small-scale version of all of this. The public key can only read (least privilege); every write goes through /api/data-write, which holds the service key on the server (Secrets Manager's job). The API secret blocks anyone without the password (a 401). Supabase secures its servers; your row-level security rules are your half of the shared responsibility.

b: AWS CloudTrail records who did what through the API (an audit trail). Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms. AWS Config records resource settings and checks them against rules. Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities. AWS Audit Manager gathers evidence for audits continuously. AWS Artifact gives you AWS's own compliance reports (SOC, ISO) on demand. AWS Trusted Advisor checks best practices. Data governance covers data lifecycle, retention, residency, lineage, cataloguing (AWS Glue Data Catalog) and access (AWS Lake Formation). The Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix sorts use cases from scope 1 (using a public consumer app) to scope 5 (training your own model); your responsibility grows with each scope.
an: Chronicles and the system_updates table are RPGACE's audit trail (CloudTrail's job). perfWatch and the error log are monitoring (CloudWatch's job). The choice to stay on Supabase Free with no backups is a governance decision you made knowingly.
